title: Design an Elevator System (OOD)
prompt: Design the control system for a building with multiple elevators. Passengers press up/down buttons on each floor and floor buttons inside each car. Model the classes, the elevator state machine, and the dispatch/scheduling logic that decides which car serves a call. Sketch the class diagram and walk through what happens when two hall calls arrive at once.
blurb: The hard OOD scheduling problem — a per-car state machine plus a pluggable dispatcher that stops two cars from chasing the same call.

rubric.label: Requirements clarification
rubric.description: Distinguishes hall calls (up/down, direction-only) from car calls (specific floor), asks about car count, express floors, capacity, and the optimization goal (wait time vs throughput vs energy).

rubric.label: Core entities
rubric.description: Identifies ElevatorSystem/Controller, ElevatorCar, Request (HallCall vs CarCall), Button/Panel, Floor, and Dispatcher/Scheduler.

rubric.label: Class design
rubric.description: Each car owns its direction, current floor, and pending-stops structure; controller separated from car; buttons modeled as request sources, not logic holders.

rubric.label: State machine
rubric.description: A clean car state machine (IDLE/MOVING_UP/MOVING_DOWN/DOORS_OPEN/MAINTENANCE) with well-defined transitions and where door timing fits.

rubric.label: Scheduling strategy
rubric.description: A pluggable dispatch policy (nearest-car / SCAN-LOOK / directional) with a clear cost function; explains why one car is chosen and how starvation is avoided.

rubric.label: Design patterns
rubric.description: Strategy for dispatch, State for the car, Observer/command for button events; each justified.

rubric.label: Relationships
rubric.description: Controller aggregates cars; car composes a request queue; correct multiplicities and ownership.

rubric.label: API methods
rubric.description: requestElevator(floor, direction), selectFloor(car, floor), step/tick, and car status queries; sensible signatures.

rubric.label: Concurrency
rubric.description: Two hall calls or two cars racing the same call; how the controller assigns exactly once; simulation loop vs event-driven; thread-safe request queues.

rubric.label: Extensibility
rubric.description: Express elevators, service/freight modes, VIP/priority calls, or a new scheduling algorithm drop in without rewriting the controller.

rubric.label: Edge cases
rubric.description: Overloaded car, call while doors closing, direction reversal mid-travel, maintenance mode, all cars busy, idle parking.

rubric.label: Communication
rubric.description: Reasons about the dispatch decision aloud, keeps the state machine legible, and handles the double-call probe without hand-waving.

functional_requirements: Passengers issue hall calls (floor + up/down direction) and car calls (target floor inside a car)
Controller dispatches one of N cars to serve each hall call
Each car moves floor-by-floor, opens/closes doors, and services pending stops in a sensible order
Cars report state (floor, direction, door state) for displays
Support idle parking and maintenance/out-of-service mode
nonfunctional_requirements: Minimize average passenger wait and total travel time
No starvation — every call is eventually served
Exactly-once assignment: two cars never both commit to the same hall call
Extensible dispatch algorithm and car modes (express, freight)
Deterministic, testable simulation via a tick/step model
clarifying_questions: How many cars and floors? Any express or restricted floors?
Are we optimizing average wait time, throughput, or energy?
Is this a real-time controller or a simulated stepped model for the interview?
Do we model door-open dwell time and car capacity/overload?
Priority calls (VIP, firefighter, freight) in scope?
Should idle cars return to a parking/lobby floor?

core_classes.name: ElevatorSystem / Controller
core_classes.responsibility: Top coordinator: receives hall calls, runs the Dispatcher to assign a car, advances the simulation, exposes status.

core_classes.name: ElevatorCar
core_classes.responsibility: One car: owns its state machine, current floor, direction, and the set of pending stops; moves one floor per tick and manages doors.

core_classes.name: Request (abstract)
core_classes.responsibility: Base for a service request; HallCall(floor, direction) from a landing, CarCall(floor) from inside a car.

core_classes.name: HallCall / CarCall
core_classes.responsibility: Concrete request subtypes; HallCall carries a desired direction, CarCall a target floor.

core_classes.name: Dispatcher (interface)
core_classes.responsibility: Pluggable scheduling policy: choose which car should serve a hall call.

core_classes.name: ElevatorState (enum/State objects)
core_classes.responsibility: IDLE, MOVING_UP, MOVING_DOWN, DOORS_OPEN, MAINTENANCE — encapsulate per-state behavior/transitions.

core_classes.name: Panel / Button
core_classes.responsibility: Input surfaces: hall panel emits HallCalls, car panel emits CarCalls; buttons hold no scheduling logic.

relationships: Controller aggregates ElevatorCar (1..*) and has-a Dispatcher (Strategy)
ElevatorCar composes its pending-stops structure and current ElevatorState
Floor has-a hall Panel; each ElevatorCar has-a car Panel
Dispatcher depends on ElevatorCar's cost estimate but not its internals (asks car.estimateCostFor)

design_patterns.why: Swap scheduling algorithms without touching the controller or cars; the optimization goal can change per building.

design_patterns.where: ElevatorState controlling car behavior and legal transitions
design_patterns.why: Keeps movement/door logic per-state instead of a giant conditional; illegal transitions become impossible.

design_patterns.where: Button presses generating Request objects and displays observing car state
design_patterns.why: Decouples input surfaces and displays from the controller.
One control system per building — but keep it injectable for testing/simulation.

apis: void requestElevator(int floor, Direction dir) — enqueues a HallCall, dispatcher assigns a car
void selectFloor(int carId, int floor) — a CarCall from inside a car
void step() — advance all cars one tick (deterministic simulation)
List<CarStatus> status() — floor/direction/door state per car
state_transitions: IDLE --hall/car call above--> MOVING_UP; --call below--> MOVING_DOWN
MOVING_UP --reached a stop--> DOORS_OPEN --dwell elapsed--> (more up stops? MOVING_UP : reverse or IDLE)
MOVING_UP/DOWN --no pending stops--> IDLE (optionally return to parking floor)
edge_cases: Overloaded car: canAccept returns false; dispatcher skips it and picks another
Hall call arrives while doors are closing at that exact floor — reopen vs treat as next stop
Direction reversal: don't reverse until all stops in the current direction are cleared (LOOK)
All cars busy — queue the call and assign when a car frees up; avoid starvation with age-based priority
Maintenance mode mid-trip: finish current passengers, then go out of service
Idle parking: spread idle cars across the building to cut future wait
concurrency: Two hall calls arrive simultaneously: the controller processes assignment serially (single-threaded dispatch loop or a lock around selectCar) so each call gets exactly one car
Preventing two cars from committing to the same call: the controller — not the cars — owns assignment; a car only receives a stop after the dispatcher commits it, so there is no race between cars
Thread-safe request intake: hall/car calls land on a concurrent queue drained by the dispatch loop; car step() reads its own stops
Real hardware is event-driven with per-car threads; for the interview prefer a deterministic single-threaded tick loop and note the locking needed if cars run concurrently
extensibility: New scheduling algorithm: implement Dispatcher (e.g., energy-aware or ML-predicted) — controller unchanged
Express elevators / restricted floors: a car carries a serviceableFloors set; canAccept checks it
Priority calls (VIP, firefighter): a PriorityDispatcher or a priority field on Request that pre-empts
Freight/service mode: a car mode enum; dispatcher filters eligible cars
Multiple banks/zones: group cars into banks, each with its own dispatcher

deep_dives.probe: Two people on floors 3 and 7 press up at the same instant. Walk me through exactly how the controller assigns cars so two cars don't both head to floor 3 and none to 7.
Your nearest-car heuristic can send a downward car to an upward call. What's the actual cost function — do you factor direction, current load, and stops already committed?
How does a single car order its pending stops? Why TreeSets split by direction (LOOK) rather than FIFO, and how do you avoid oscillation?
Under heavy load, a top-floor down call keeps getting outbid. How do you guarantee it's eventually served?

followup_bank.question: Nearest-by-distance ignores direction and load. What does your full cost function look like, and where does that live — a Dispatcher Strategy?
FIFO makes a car pass floors it should stop at. How do you order stops so the car sweeps in one direction (SCAN/LOOK)?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions state or moving or idle
followup_bank.question: Model that as an explicit State machine — what are the legal transitions and where does door-dwell time sit?
If each car runs on its own thread, what stops two cars from grabbing the same call — where's the single point of assignment?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions priority or vip or emergency
followup_bank.question: How do you inject priority/pre-emption without special-casing it throughout the controller?

tradeoffs: Nearest-car (simple, low latency) vs SCAN/LOOK (higher throughput, fairer) vs load-aware (best UX, more state)
Single-threaded tick simulation (deterministic, testable) vs per-car threads (realistic, needs locking)
Controller-owns-assignment (no inter-car race, central bottleneck) vs cars-bid (distributed, risk of double-commit)
Returning idle cars to lobby (faster peak response) vs staying put (less wasted movement)
reference.reference_answer: A strong senior answer separates the ElevatorSystem/Controller (owns cars + a pluggable Dispatcher) from each ElevatorCar (owns its State machine and direction-split stop sets). Hall calls and car calls are distinct Request subtypes. The controller — not the cars — commits an assignment, which is the crux of why two cars never chase the same call: assignment is serialized through the dispatch loop. The Dispatcher is a Strategy with a real cost function over distance, direction, and committed load (nearest-car as a baseline, SCAN/LOOK for fairness), and the candidate explains starvation avoidance via call aging. The car uses a State pattern with clear IDLE/MOVING/DOORS_OPEN/MAINTENANCE transitions and LOOK-style stop ordering. They pick a deterministic tick simulation for testability while noting the locking real per-car threads would need, handle overload/maintenance/reversal edge cases, and show extensibility to express cars, priority calls, and new algorithms without editing the controller.

interviewer_notes: This is senior — expect a real scheduling story, not just classes. Let them clarify hall-vs-car calls and the optimization goal first. The make-or-break probe is the simultaneous double hall call: push until they articulate that the controller serializes assignment (so cars can't double-commit) and that the dispatch cost function considers direction and load, not just distance. Insist on an explicit car State machine — if they bury movement in if/else, ask them to draw the transitions and place door-dwell. Then push stop ordering (LOOK vs FIFO) and starvation. Over-engineering traps to flag: per-car threads with elaborate locking when a tick simulation is cleaner for an interview, a pub/sub event bus before the core dispatch works, or ML/energy optimization before a correct baseline. If time remains, ask for the express-elevator or priority-call extension to test that Dispatcher and canAccept keep the controller closed for modification.
